pitch_detail.notes: Duckabush Trailhead to the LaCrosse Pass Trail junction via Duckabush River Trail #803, roughly 15-16 miles with about 3,600 ft of gain over the Little/Big Hump benches.
LaCrosse Pass Trail over the Duckabush/West Fork Dosewallips divide, about 6.4 miles with roughly 2,000 ft of gain.
Off-trail talus and heather ridge running roughly a mile south from near LaCrosse Pass to the summit; no roped climbing, straightforward route-finding in good visibility.
Maintained High Pass Trail via Low Pass then High Pass, roughly 2.3 miles one-way; can hold snow/avalanche debris into summer.
Leave the trail near 6,400 ft, traverse/descend about 100-200 ft into the basin, then ascend boulder fields, scree, and dirt to the southwest spur near 6,900 ft.
pitch_detail.pitch: High Pass basin to SW spur

pitch_detail.notes: Two narrow gully channels about 30 ft apart split the rocky face; take the right-hand one, ascending narrow then open gully through loose, broken rock to the ridge crest.
Follow the ridge crest, favoring the west side, to the summit.

itinerary.cal: Twin Lakes Rd (FS 3065) can be rough or seasonally gated below the lakes, and the gully often holds snow into July, favoring an ice axe/microspikes for early-season attempts.

days.note: From the Twin Lakes trailhead, follow the High Pass trail north over Low Pass and High Pass, then leave the trail around 6,400 ft and traverse/descend slightly into the basin below Larrabee's south face. Scramble scree and boulders to a gully system at ~6,900 ft (take the right-hand of two narrow chutes), climb loose rock to gain the south ridge, then follow the ridge crest (favoring the west side) to the summit. Descend by reversing the route — the loose, chossy rock makes the descent nearly as slow as the ascent, and a helmet is considered mandatory due to rockfall.
days.title: Twin Lakes to summit and back, car-to-car

schedule.label: Leave trailhead area
schedule.detail: Twin Lakes Rd is rough/rutted and sometimes gated below the lakes; if impassable, park near Yellow Aster Butte TH, adding ~2.3 mi each way and ~1,500 ft of climbing on the walk in.

schedule.label: Twin Lakes, start High Pass trail
schedule.detail: Head north past the lakes toward Low Pass then High Pass.

schedule.label: Leave trail, enter south-face basin
schedule.detail: Around 6,400 ft, traverse and drop slightly into the basin facing Larrabee's south side.

schedule.label: Ascend the gully
schedule.detail: At ~6,900 ft find the two narrow parallel chutes; take the right-hand one, staying climber's right on better rock, to broken terrain and the ridge crest.

schedule.label: Summit (7,865 ft)
schedule.detail: Follow the ridge, favoring the west side, to the top.

schedule.label: Back at trailhead
schedule.detail: Reverse the full route; loose rock makes downclimbing the gully slow and rockfall-prone.

days.objective: Summit Mount Larrabee via the South Ridge gully

itinerary.totalNote: A single long day car-to-car: roughly 8 miles round trip with about 4,200 ft of gain, typically 7-9 hours including a slow, loose descent; strong parties have done it in 6, casual parties closer to 9-10.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September; August is the most reliable window

July.reason: Season opens mid-July; early in the month snow can linger and rivers may still run high

June.reason: Trail network and approach terrain still largely snowbound at elevation; river fords are dangerous with peak snowmelt (outside the season window)

August.reason: Most stable weather and driest approach/scramble conditions of the year

October.reason: Falls outside the season; full winter conditions can arrive on this long, remote approach

September.reason: Still within the season; cooler and generally stable, but early-season snow becomes a real possibility by late month

climate.fall: Cooling temperatures with increasing rain by October; fords can rise again with early storms.
climate.spring: Trail can still hold snow above the mid-elevation sections into June, and fords typically run high with snowmelt.
climate.summer: The driest and most reliable season (roughly June/July–September), though brush remains thick on the off-trail scramble portion.
climate.winter: Heavy valley rain and higher-elevation snow; the access road may be closed or restricted.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate — Pacific storm fronts drive heavy orographic precipitation across the Olympic interior; the Quinault valley is one of the wettest corridors in the range

bySeason.fall: Rain returns by September/October and river fords become riskier with rising flows
bySeason.spring: Trail still snow-covered at upper elevations; North Shore Road can be affected by spring washouts
bySeason.summer: Driest and most reliable window (June–August); the ascent chute can still hold snow into June
bySeason.winter: Heavy snow and near-constant rain at low elevation; road/trail access frequently disrupted
